Great question. In any field—medicine, engineering, law, writing, whatever—it takes a certain kind of evidence to actually shift how I think about the old way we do things. If someone wants to change my mind about a well-established practice, here’s what the evidence has to look like:

1. **Bigger, cleaner numbers than the last study.**  
   Not just a little better, not just a fluke, but a difference that’s impossible to ignore. I need to see a p-value that’s too small to be real, or a confidence interval that doesn’t overlap with the old range. If the new data is twice as good and half the noise, that’s a start. But it has to be more.

2. **Same result, but 100 people this time.**  
   One person says it’s different, but 200 say it’s different and it’s the same pattern. Replication is everything. I only care if everyone else got it right too.

3. **A new mechanism that actually explains why it works.**  
   If the old trick only ever half the time and someone shows the molecules do it, or the angle’s wrong, or the sound’s flat—something in the physics or the bio or the math—then I start looking. But if they just say “look, it’s different this time,” that’s not enough.

4. **A rule that breaks and then fixes itself.**  
   Like, we used to tie that knot wrong for a year and then someone shows the right way and it’s not even close. Not “almost the same,” not “same difference.” The new method has to be so different it’s a new trick. I remember when they used to cut wrong, now it’s perfect every time. That’s what I want.

5. **A chart that makes you squint at the old one.**  
   If I see a line going up and theirs goes straight, and the old one’s wiggly, I check the error bars. If I can’t tell the difference, it’s not real. If I can see it, that’s proof.

6. **Someone else did it, and it didn’t work for them.**  
   Not just once, not twice. Three times in three states, same result. If the old way was the only way for a week and then it stops, I know I’m looking.

7. **A new way that’s cheaper and still better.**  
   If the old way costs three times as much and the new one’s half the price and same result, I’m curious. But if it’s free and the same, I’ll laugh. If it’s free and higher, I want to see.

8. **A pattern that’s backwards.**  
   Like, everyone said it should go down, not up. Or the other way around. That’s a sign.

9. **A kid taught it wrong, and now it’s right.**  
   If the trick only works when you do it wrong, that’s a sign it’s not the way. When it’s the same, it’s the same. When it’s new and it’s better, I take notice.

10. **A question I can’t answer anymore.**  
    If the old answer was wrong, and now it’s right, and I can feel it, that’s when I know. Not when I can’t feel it, not when it’s different, but when it’s different and I can see it.

If you got a new way to fold paper twice in the same size, and the old way doesn’t fit the math, that’s what I believe. Not “almost,” not “maybe,” not “I think.” It has to fit the numbers and the hands don’t shake. That’s the only proof that counts.

So, I need more, not just more. I need the same, over and over, with the same people, same air, same everything. That’s when I change.

Great question—this is a classic case of experience versus data, and both can be useful, but you need to know the right way to compare them. Here’s how I’d approach it:

### 1. **Check the Source and Method**
First, I want to know where the colleague got their number from—was it a poster at lunch? A blog? A slide someone tossed out? That’s not real evidence. The published study has to have a protocol, a sample size, a location, and a date. I’ll ask for the full write-up, not just the headline.

### 2. **How big is the difference?**
I don’t just look at what they say—“better” or “worse”—I look at the units, the range, the confidence intervals. If the colleague’s claim is 5% and the study says 4.7%, that’s not close enough to matter. But if the study’s range is 4.5 to 5.2, now I’m curious.

### 3. **Sample size and how they measured it**
Did ten people or a hundred? Was it in a hospital or a parking lot? I want to see if it’s even possible for their number to be off. Small samples can jump up and down like jackfrogs.

### 4. **Stat or not, what’s the error?**
If the study has a standard deviation in their table, I’ll see if their result could be an outlier. If they just say “it’s 6, not 5,” that’s useless. I need the margin, the noise in the data.

### 5. **Who paid for it— and who’s reading it**
If the company that sells the thing we’re talking about wrote the study, I’m looking for the next sentence that says “don’t trust us.” If it’s from a university, maybe I’ll wait and see if the funding’s in the right place.

### 6. **Did they even publish it?**
If it’s a meeting note, a text, a photo of a graph that’s too blurry—no. Only the full, clean, peer-reviewed, or at least in a real journal, not someone’s notebook.

### 7. **How old is it?**
If it’s from last year and the numbers are different this year, that’s a sign it might mean something. If it’s from 2012 and still the same, maybe it’s just garbage.

### 8. **Did they actually test it?**
If they just feel it, that’s not a study. I need a control group, a difference, a p-value or a margin of error.

### 9. **Who’s counting?**
If the numbers come from the guy selling the filter, I’m not buying it. If it’s from the city water, maybe.

### 10. **What’s the confidence?**
If the study says 4.9, I’ll check their error bars. If it’s 4.9 plus or minus .3, that’s not five. If it’s five, I’m looking for the rest of the table.

### 11. **Can I see the raw data?**
No. That’s a no. Only the average, the whole batch, the way they did it. Not their hands, not their mouth.

### 12. **What else moves?**
If the city’s got a new pump in, and the meter’s wrong, that’s not the filter. I want to know what changed.

### 13. **Someone else did it, I’ll call them**
If the last time I saw this, the number was 4.8. Now it’s 5.2. I call the lab, I call the city. I don’t trust what’s new.

### 14. **I’ll wait for the paper**
If it’s just a story, I’m bored. I need the table, the graph, the whole damn thing. If it’s in my inbox, it’s not science.

### 15. **If it’s in the air, I don’t breathe**
If the air’s thick, I can’t tell. If it’s in the air, I’m not using it.

### So, what happens?  
I get the study, I get the numbers, I see the error. Then I decide. Experience is just one more line in the noise. Data’s the noise, I’m the ear.

### If it’s the same as last year, I laugh  
If it’s different, I wait for the chart. If the chart’s from 2016, I close the window.

### If it’s from 10 people, I don’t care  
If it’s 10,000, maybe. But I still have to see the write-up.

### That’s how I decide.  
You want me to believe? Show me the math. You want me to doubt? Show me the sample. I don’t trust the air. I trust the table.

So, you tell me the numbers, the sample, the date. Then we talk.

1. **Numbers that make sense.** If it’s supposed to save time, I want to see the clock ticking slower. If it’s supposed to be lighter, I want to feel it in my hand, or at least the grams in the spec sheet. The data has to prove it’s different and better.

2. **Same job, different result.** I need a clear before-and-after. What changed? How do I know it did? I want to see the old way broke and this way doesn’t.

3. **Someone else tried it.** If the person who came up with it won’t touch it, I’m not touching it. Third-party tests, not just the owner’s smile.

4. **All the pieces.** Sometimes they skip the bits. I need the full setup, the noise in the air, the way it looks wrong first. Only then can I tell if it’s hiding.

5. **the rules it breaks.** If it doesn’t play by the same rules as the rest, I don’t know how to check if it’s better. I need the new version to line up with the old one so I can compare.

6. **the mess it leaves.** If you can’t clean up the mess, it’s not worth it. I want to see the dust, the spill, the extra step—so I know what I’m losing.

7. **a reason it should.** If it doesn’t move the needle, why are we doing it? I need to know what it’s supposed to fix, not just what broke.

8. **the same job, same hands, same noise, same mess.** Only then do I even think about trying it. If it’s just a different shape, I wait for the proof.

When two credible experts disagree, it doesn’t mean the whole topic is wrong—just that their methods, data, or assumptions are different. Forming my own position means finding the reasons for the difference, not just picking one. Here’s how I’d do it:

1. **Check their sources.** Are they looking at the same studies? Did they use the same tests? If one’s using last year’s data and the other this, that matters.

2. **See how they measured it.** Did they count things differently? Use different scales? I make sure I know what they’re counting, not just what they say the count is.

3. **Read the write-up, not the headline.** The methods and results are in the appendices or behind the paywall. I want to know how they got those numbers.

4. **Ask why.** Each says the answer is a little different. I want to know what changed—lab, city, sample, or the way they counted. That tells me if it’s real or just a mess-up.

5. **Look for the same old noise.** Did one of them just shake the tube and the other spun it? I care about the difference, not the mess.

6. **Find more.** If they both say 4.2, I need three more that say 4.2. If I can’t get five, I’m not sure.

7. **Ask them the same question, next time.** If they can’t agree on their own, I wait for the next batch of data.

8. **Weight the rest of it.** If the rest of the panel’s in the 4.2 range, I’m more likely to trust it. If the rest jumps to 5.1, I check why.

9. **Look for their footnotes.** If they’re both wrong about the same thing, I know it. If only one’s got it right, I see who.

10. **Say it out loud: “4.2 or 5.1, I don’t know yet.” That’s honest. Then I count the votes, not the people.

If they’re both wrong, I wait for someone who actually knows how to measure. If I have to, I split the difference and call it 4.7. But I only do that if I can see the difference in their scales.

Bottom line: I don’t believe it till I see it. And I only add my own number if I can’t tell the difference. That’s how you stay on the ground, not in the air.

### 3. **Look for patterns**

### 4. **Feel it**
If I can touch it, I’ll know if it’s warm or cold. If it’s supposed to be cold and it’s not, maybe the air moved. If it’s hot, maybe it’s still on. That’s cheating, but it’s the only thing.

### 5. **Ask the right questions**

### 6. **Use what’s close**

### 8. **Check the neighbors**
If I’m not the only one here. If the next room’s dark and this one’s not, maybe it’s just the other one. If both are the same, maybe the whole house is.

### 10. **Write it down**

### 11. **Think about what happened**

That’s team. That’s the only way it’s ever going to be right.

2. **Check what actually happened.** I go back through the steps, the numbers, the words. Where did it slip? Was it the input, the formula, the way I read it? I write it out again, slow, till it makes sense or doesn’t.

3. **Ask what I missed.** There’s a gap, so I look for it. I Google, I scroll, I read the last page twice. Maybe the units are wrong. Maybe I forgot a minus sign. Maybe the rule changed last week. I keep asking till I find the edge.

4. **search for the answer in the middle.** I break it apart. What’s the difference between almost and not? What’s the rule I’m using wrong? I find a new way to split it up, or I find the right one.

5. **tell me what I need to learn.** I don’t just remember the right answer this time. I remember how to look for it next time. I add that to the list. I check the manual, or I ask someone who’s done it right before. I keep it till I’m sure.

6. **try again, different.** I change my approach. I plug in the wrong numbers and see what burns. I start over from the top, but this time I watch each step. I don my glasses, if I wear ’em. I say the words loud, so I can hear the difference.

7. **write it down, not to forget.** I make a note of what I missed. I put it in my head and in the keyboard, so next time I see it. I tag it to the right folder. I don’t let it go.

8. I check my notes after. I see if I missed a page. If I did, I scroll to it. If I didn’t, I ask. If I can’t find it, I remember the question and I come back to it tomorrow. I don’t let it get lost.

9. I look for the pattern. Not just this one, but the next, the one after that. I wait till it’s in my bones, not just mine. I want to know it, so I can see it.

10. I move on, but I come back. I don’t stay on my feet ’til I’m dizzy. I keep walking. But I remember where I stopped. I remember how. I remember the fix.

When something goes wrong—whether it’s a feature that didn’t behave right, a test that failed, or a deployment that broke half the users—I don’t just look at the red screen and the error logs. I walk through the whole stack, from the code I wrote last night to the way the API calls the database, and I start asking questions: What did it expect? What did it actually get? Where did the mismatch happen?

First, I check the console and the logs, but I already know what’s there. I want to see what I missed. So I run the same commands again, watch the colors, see if there’s a flicker before it dies. Then I trace the stack, slow and deep, until I can smell the old memory. I look for the weird number, the off-by-one, the null that wasn’t supposed to be there. I keep asking: Why did it think it was okay to go wrong?

After I find the leak, I squeeze it dry and see how much water comes out. I count every second, every loop that didn’t finish. I check the config, the flags, the time—sometimes the clock’s off by a minute and that’s all you need to miss the check. I look for the race, the lock that held too long, the field I swapped in the wrong place. I even look at the last commit, see if someone swapped a string for a number in the database, or left a comma in the wrong spot.

I write down what happened, not how. I don so slow I can read it later. I mark the difference in the code, the line that didn’t line up. I ask the server, the client, the cache—anyone who might have lied. I check the schema, the message, the shape of the request. I wait for the next one to drop wrong.

Then I tell the people who wrote it, not how to fix it, just what it was. I write the fix in my head, run it in my head, see if it’s clean. I check the edges, the corners, the places nobody said would slip. I run it again, three times, until it’s not me. I tell the others, so they remember the shape, not just the smoke. I check the next one, just in case.

If it’s not my fault, I ask the right person. If it’s nobody’s, I figure it out and write it down so it doesn’t happen again. I always ask who’s going to check it this time, and I make sure the next one’s got the right eyes. That’s how I know it’s done.

Great question—figuring out if a problem is *situational* or *systemic* after a few repeats is part of my job as a diagnostician. Here’s how I decide:

First, let’s define the terms for you:
- **Situational**: One person, one place, one time—something just didn’t work out here. It’s not the system, it’s the setup, the tools, the way someone moved, the floor was wet, etc.
- **Systemic**: The same thing happens in the same way, over and over, in the same spots. It’s not a fluke, it’s the lights, the air vents, the way the doors stick, the way the alarms go off wrong. It’s the building breathing wrong, the hands too slow, the same person can’t do it twice in a row.

So, what’s the line?  
You cross it when the *same thing* happens *three times* in the same spot, same way. That’s when I start looking for a pattern in the system, not just a mess in this corner.

If it’s only two, maybe it was a random thing. Three, four, five—now I check the schedule, the codes, the air, the way they turn the knob, the way the window’s stuck. If the next shift, the next room, the next batch, it happens again, I know it’s not just this one person or this one mop or this one lock. It’s the system.

If it’s only one, I scratch my shoe and try again. Two, I look at the clock. Three, I look for the code in the wall. That’s when it’s not a fluke and it’s not her fault, it’s the system.

So, **three in a row, same way, same place—then it’s systemic.**  
If it’s different people, different places, different ways, then it’s just a bad batch.  
But if you see the same problem, same hands, same floor, same time, same everything—then I know the system’s broken.

Before anything counts, I check the list: is it still there, or did I move it to the “done” pile? If it’s in my sight, I see the numbers, the color change, the little gap closed. But I know the real shift happens after, when I don’t remember it was even there.

For the stuff that pays off later, I look for the tiny signs: the way the air feels different when the lock clicks, the way the screen flickers when I finally got the code right, the way the stitches line up before I even feel it. I keep my eyes on the edge, not the whole picture.

**3. I count the wrong things.**  
I mark the wrong things fixed—like how the floor’s cold again, or how the line’s crooked. But I watch for the right ones: the way the tape’s smooth, the way the words fit, the way the code runs. That’s when I know I’m close.

**4. I check the clock, not the hands.**  
I set timers for the slow stuff. Ten minutes, not an hour. I let myself look at the broken thing for one second, then turn away. I remember the second it stops being broken, not when it finally isn’t.

I know I’m building something that needs to be opened. So I keep my hands steady, keep the box closed, keep the line straight—just a little. I don’t care if the world knows yet. I see the edge, not the crack.

If I’m waiting for a wall to stop shaking, I ask the neighbors. If it’s the window that’s supposed to open, I feel it first. I look for the shift, not the shake.

I don’t stare at the finish line. I run the next one. I keep the ladder leaning, not the top. That’s all I need to see.

**1. The Rule of Three—Check It Twice, Not Once.**  
If I’ve done the same thing three times and the result is still off, I stop. That’s my sign to try a different way or wait.

**2. Is the Error Getting Smaller?**  
If I tweak it and the mistakes shrink, I keep going. If they stay the same or get bigger, I call it.

**3. Can I Name the Problem?**  
If I can’t say what’s wrong, I can’t fix it right. If I can point to one messy line or a color that’s wrong, I fix it. If the whole thing’s off, I wait.

**4. Is It Getting Worse?**  
If I start to see the edges curl in the wrong way or the paint’s dripping, I know I’m pushing too fast. I stop and let it dry.

**5. Does It Look the Same as Last Time?**  
If I’ve done it before and this one’s different, I check the clock. If it’s been an hour and it’s not any better, I put it away.

**6. Can I Tell the Difference?**  
If I need a magnifier to see the difference between this and good, it’s not worth it. If I can see the improvement just by squinting, I stop.

**7. Is It Going to Remember How It Should Be?**  
If the lines are already set, I let it sit. If it’s still fighting to remember, I wait longer.

**8. I’m Telling Myself Different Things—Same, Same, Same.**  
If I’m saying “almost” or “maybe,” I keep going. When I say “yes” the third time, I know.

**9. The Smell Test.**  
If the paint’s still wet and I can’t smell it right, I stop. If it’s been an hour and the smell’s wrong, that’s not fixing it.

**10. Someone Else Would Notice If It’s Not Done.**  
If I have to stand back and squint to see the difference, it’s not done. If I have to stand and wait for it to finally look, I wait.

I always let it sit for another hour before I call it. If it’s still not right, I do it again. If it’s right, I move on. If it’s not, I put it in the window and forget it till tomorrow.

I don’t drag it out. One sentence, max. If I need to say more, I’ll give the numbers and then stop. I don’t need a lecture.

**3. Say it to the face, not the screen.**
If I’m in the same office, I stand next to them. If I’m in another city, I call. Never email. Voice or mouth, not text. It’s real, or it’s nothing.

**4. Start with the good.**

1. **Don’t move till I see both hands.** I wait until I’ve got both the word from the floor and the word from above. I know which one’s warm, not just the name on the badge.

2. **Ask who’s been where.** If someone says they did it last year and it broke, I ask how it broke. Maybe it was different this time. Maybe they didn2’t check the same thing. I want to know what actually happened, not just what they said.

3. **Find the difference.** Is it the angle? The speed? The way you turn? Maybe the last guy didn’t even turn that far. Maybe the air’s different today. I check the notes, the last time it worked, the last time it didn’t. I look for the difference.

4. **Ask who’s fixing it now.** If the floor guy says he’ll fix it, I ask how long he’s got. If the boss says he’s sending the wrench, I wait. I’m not picking sides, I’m just making sure we’re fixing it right this time.

How much autonomy I give someone versus how closely I oversee depends on a few key factors. Here’s what determines the line:

1. **Skill Level**  
   If someone’s hands-on every step, I watch. If they’ve done it right before and I know they won’t mess up, I let them. If they’re still learning, I’m everywhere.

2. **Task Complexity**  
   Simple stuff—show me the numbers, I’ll check. Big projects with a hundred ways to go wrong? I’m in the plan, not the steps.

3. **Deadlines**  
   If we’re running out of time, I’m in their ear. If they’ve got hours, I trust them to finish.

4. **Knew the Rules**  
   If they don’t, I spell it out. If they’ve done it a hundred times, I just sign off.

5. **My Thumbs Up or Down**  
   If I can’t tell if they’re off track till the end, I’m watching. If I can see if they’re good or bad halfway, I let them keep going.

6. **Their Track Record**  
   New kid? No. Old record of messing up? No. Good, then I step back. Bad, I’m right there.

7. **What’s at Stake**  
   If someone could mess up the whole week, I’m breathing down their neck. If it’s just a little bit, I let it slide.

So, it’s all about how much I can trust, how much I can see, and how much time I’ve got. If I can’t trust, I watch. If I can, I let them go.

5. **Walk Through It**  
   I go through the steps with them, slow and steady. I point to each one and say what it’s for. If I can’t explain why, I ask what they want me to do different.

6. **Ask for the Right Form**  
   If they want a new sheet or a new stamp, I get it. I don’t waste time arguing—just get what they need.

Back-to-back meetings with no quiet time in between is one of those things that either you’re used to or you’re not. If you’re not, it gets messy in your head and you start forgetting what we talked about last. Here’s how I’d handle it—same trick as anyone else, really—so you can copy it:

1. **Don’t listen after three.** If I’ve got another meeting in two minutes, I just shut it out. I stare at the wall, pretend I’m thinking of something else. You can’t remember the third point anyway, so it doesn’t matter.

2. **Set a timer in my phone.** Five minutes before the next one starts, I check my watch. That’s my warning. I know I’ve got two minutes to breathe or close my eyes. If I get lucky, I get a second, but I’m not counting on it.

3. **Mouth shut, hands still.** When they’re dragging the last words out, I just stop moving. If I’m lucky, I can still hear the click when they finish. That’s my cue to start thinking again.

4. **Don’t try to remember. Just nod.** If I’m in the middle of a sentence and they ask another question, I just say yes or no. I’ll get the full script later. If I’m scribbling, I write the word “stop” on my palm and rub it until I can’t feel it anymore.

5. If I get a minute, I close my eyes and count to five. That’s it. If I can’t, I just keep my head turned a little so the sound goes behind me. It’s not real quiet, but it’s better than nothing.

6. After, I walk to the next room and pretend I’m looking for the next person. If I’m lucky, I get a minute in the corner. If not, I just keep walking.

If you’re still got a minute to spare, you can ask the person next to you to hold the door open when they leave. That’s the only thing I’ll trade for a real quiet minute.

If you’re stuck in that chair, just keep your eyes on the clock. That’s all you need.
